title: Visual Pathways
subtitle: Reading a visual field defect, acuity change and pupil sign to place the lesion from retina to occipital cortex

points.text: Temporal-retina axons stay ipsilateral to the lateral geniculate body, while nasal-retina axons cross at the chiasm.
points.quote: The axons of the ganglion cells on the temporal side of a vertical line drawn through the fovea project to the ipsilateral lateral geniculate body

points.text: At the chiasm slightly more than half of the fibers cross (53:47), and these come from the nasal retina.
points.quote: more than half of the fibers (those originating in ganglion cells of the nasal retina) cross to reach the contralateral optic tract

points.text: The crossed:uncrossed ratio in the chiasm is a number worth remembering for chiasmal field analysis.
points.quote: The ratio of crossed and uncrossed fibers in the chiasm is 53:47.

points.text: Retinal nerve fibers respect the horizontal meridian only in the nasal visual field, because the raphe lies in the temporal retina.
points.quote: the nerve fiber layer of the retina respects the horizontal meridian only in the nasal field, not in the temporal field

points.text: The LGN is a thalamic relay for all retinal ganglion cell axons that subserve vision.
points.quote: The lateral geniculate body, a thalamic nucleus, provides a relay station for all the axons of the retinal ganglion cells subserving vision.

points.text: LGN laminae alternate between the two eyes: I, IV and VI are contralateral, II, III and V ipsilateral.
points.quote: Layers I, IV, and VI serve the contralateral eye, whereas II, III, and V are connected with the ipsilateral eye.

points.text: Upper-field fibers go through the parietal lobe.
points.quote: Upper field fibers originate in the medial aspect of lateral geniculate nucleus and travel through the parietal lobes

points.text: Lower-field fibers loop through the temporal lobe (Meyer loop).
points.quote: lower field fibers originate from the lateral aspect of the lateral geniculate body and make a loop in the temporal lobe

points.text: Primary visual cortex (area 17) lies along the calcarine fissure on the medial occipital surface.
points.quote: Cortical area 17 of Brodmann, located along the superior and inferior lips of the calcarine fissure in the medial aspect of the occipital lobe

points.text: Each occipital lobe sees the opposite visual hemifield, because it receives the same-side half of each retina.
points.quote: More simply, it receives projections from the two halves of the retinas on the same side as the occipital lobe

points.text: Macula is represented posteriorly, periphery anteriorly in the calcarine cortex.
points.quote: the macular retina is represented in the posterior pole of the calcarine cortex, whereas the more peripheral retina is more anteriorly represented

points.text: Complete central retinal artery occlusion gives global retinal ischemia unless a cilioretinal artery supplies the macula.
points.quote: the complete occlusion of the central retinal artery results in global retinal ischemia, except when the macular area is supplied by cilioretinal arteries

points.text: The optic tract also receives the anterior choroidal artery, a branch of the internal carotid.
points.quote: which, in addition, is fed by the anterior choroidal artery, a branch of the internal carotid

points.text: The LGN has a dual supply: anterior choroidal laterally, lateral posterior choroidal medially.
points.quote: The lateral geniculate body receives a dual supply, from the anterior choroidal artery laterally and the lateral posterior choroidal artery medially.

points.text: The upper radiations are supplied by the middle cerebral artery, the lower by the posterior cerebral artery.
points.quote: The upper (parietal) portion of the optic radiations is supplied by branches of the middle cerebral artery

points.text: The calcarine branch of the PCA supplies the primary visual cortex.
points.quote: The posterior cerebral artery, particularly its calcarine branch running in the calcarine fissure, supplies the primary visual cortex.

localizationRules.explanation: A monocular field defect points to the retina or optic nerve; a binocular defect places the lesion at or beyond the chiasm.
localizationRules.quote: whether the field defect is monocular, in which case the lesion usually affects the retina or the optic nerve, or binocular

localizationRules.explanation: Most optic neuropathies reduce acuity, so a visual field defect with preserved acuity should make you think of preretinal, retinal or retrochiasmal disease.
localizationRules.quote: Also, most optic neuropathies involve VA; spared acuity should raise the suspicion of preretinal, retinal, or retrochiasmal disease

localizationRules.explanation: Tract and LGN hemianopias tend to be incongruous; the further back the lesion, the more the two eyes' defects match.
localizationRules.quote: the more posteriorly the lesion is located in the optic pathways, the greater the congruity of the defect in either field

localizationRules.explanation: A tract lesion can cause a modest RAPD in the eye contralateral to the lesion (the eye with temporal field loss).
localizationRules.quote: Optic tract disease may cause a modest RAPD when the light is directed into the eye contralateral to the lesion

localizationRules.explanation: Lesions of the LGN and geniculocalcarine pathway leave the light reflex intact, because pupillary afferents leave before the LGN.
localizationRules.quote: Lateral geniculate body lesions and those in the geniculocalcarine segment of the optic sensory pathways leave the pupillary light reflex unimpaired.

keySyndromes.name: Body of the chiasm syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Bitemporal field defects (peripheral and/or central, with or without macular splitting) + usually normal visual acuity + normal or pale optic discs
keySyndromes.clue: Bitemporal defects are most often due to a compressive mass such as a pituitary tumor.
keySyndromes.quote: Body of the chiasm syndrome, in which patients demonstrate bitemporal visual field defects

keySyndromes.name: Anterior chiasm (junctional) syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Central defect in one eye + superior temporal defect in the other eye
keySyndromes.clue: Reflects damage to the ipsilateral optic nerve at its junction with the chiasm; test the field of the apparently normal eye.
keySyndromes.quote: central defect in one field with a superior temporal defect in the opposite field points to the involvement of the anterior angle of the chiasm

keySyndromes.name: Optic tract lesion
keySyndromes.triad: Incongruous homonymous hemianopia (macula-splitting if complete) + RAPD in the contralateral eye + normal visual acuity
keySyndromes.clue: Chronic lesions may produce hemianopic optic atrophy (bow-tie pallor in the contralateral eye).
keySyndromes.quote: afferent pupillary defect in the contralateral eye in a patient with normal VA bilaterally and a complete HH are usually indicative of optic tract involvement

keySyndromes.name: Lateral geniculate body: anterior choroidal artery
keySyndromes.triad: Congruous homonymous defect in upper and lower quadrants + sparing of a horizontal sector (quadruple sectoranopia) + sectorial optic atrophy
keySyndromes.clue: Posterior choroidal artery interruption instead causes a horizontal wedge-shaped sector defect.
keySyndromes.quote: Occlusion of the anterior choroidal artery may cause a homonymous defect in the upper and lower quadrants with the sparing of a horizontal sector

keySyndromes.name: Parietal optic radiations
keySyndromes.triad: Inferior quadrantic defect (pie on the floor) + more congruous than temporal lesions + other parietal signs
keySyndromes.clue: Large lesions can give complete macula-splitting hemianopia; parietal lesions more often betray themselves by other neurologic signs.
keySyndromes.quote: The involvement of the optic radiations in the depth of the parietal lobe gives rise to an inferior quadrantic defect

keySyndromes.name: Medial occipital lesion
keySyndromes.triad: Highly congruous homonymous hemianopia + macular sparing when both calcarine banks are involved + posterior cerebral artery infarct as the common cause
keySyndromes.clue: Complete HH with macular sparing points to the occipital cortex.
keySyndromes.quote: When both the upper and lower calcarine cortices are affected, a complete HH, usually with macular sparing, develops

boardTraps.text: Wilbrand knee may be an artifact of enucleation, yet junctional field loss still localizes to the junction of optic nerve and chiasm.
boardTraps.quote: whether Wilbrand knee exists anatomically, the localizing value of junctional visual field loss to the junction of the optic nerve and chiasm remains undiminished

boardTraps.text: A complete homonymous hemianopia does not localize within the retrochiasmal pathway.
boardTraps.quote: Complete HHs are nonlocalizing and may be seen with any lesion of the retrochiasmal pathway

boardTraps.text: Congruity helps but is not a strict rule: many tract and radiation lesions give congruent defects, especially after stroke.
boardTraps.quote: although lesions involving the occipital lobe characteristically produce congruent HH, at least 50% of lesions in other locations also produce congruent HH

boardTraps.text: The monocular temporal crescent is the one retrochiasmal field defect that can be strictly unilateral.
boardTraps.quote: This is the only retrochiasmatic lesion that may cause a strictly unilateral visual field defect

boardTraps.text: Bitemporal defects that cross the vertical midline are pseudochiasmal and may reflect ametropia, tilted discs or other eye disease.
boardTraps.quote: Pseudochiasmal visual field defects (i.e., bitemporal defects that do not respect the vertical midline) may also be due to ametropia

boardTraps.text: Pure occipital lesions leave the patient aware of the hemianopia; larger or more anterior lesions may not.
boardTraps.quote: Patients with purely occipital lesions are partially or fully aware of the hemianopia, whereas patients with larger or more anterior lesions
